title: Spiral Galaxy NGC 3370, Home to Supernova Seen in 1994
caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 3370, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 3370 · constellation Leo · about 98 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, The Hubble Heritage Team and A. Riess (STScI)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: The dusty spiral NGC 3370 fills the foreground, its intricate arms spotted with hot areas of new star formation, while far-off galaxies crowd the background. It lies 98 million light-years away in the constellation Leo.

In November 1994 light from an exploding star in NGC 3370 reached Earth. That supernova, SN 1994ae, for a short time outshone every other star in its galaxy, tens of billions of them. It was a type Ia supernova, the kind astronomers use to chart how fast the universe is expanding, and one of the nearest and best observed since modern digital detectors arrived.

Using type Ia supernovae as yardsticks means calibrating their true brightness. Cepheid variable stars, whose regular pulsing reveals their intrinsic brightness, can give the distance to the host galaxy directly. Adam Riess of the Space Telescope Science Institute observed NGC 3370 a dozen times over a month to follow its Cepheids, which only Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys could resolve at the time.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through visual, infrared and blue filters. The color mapping is not published.
understand.eye: About 25 hours of exposure gathered far more light than an eye ever could, which is why so many faint background galaxies appear.

behind.people: See full credit: NASA, The Hubble Heritage Team and A. Riess (STScI)
behind.exposure: Observation dates per NASA: April - May 2003, Exposure Time: 25 hours.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: All those visits added up to about one full day of exposure, making this one of Hubble's deepest views and bringing thousands of background galaxies into sight. Riess needed only two filters, covering visual and infrared light, and the Hubble Heritage Project added a blue filter to make the color picture. His Cepheids here were the most distant yet observed with Hubble.
alt: A dusty spiral galaxy with intricate arms in the foreground, set against a backdrop of many distant galaxies.
